issues.item: Triggers: Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
issues.explanation: For terrorism trauma in a 70-year-old civilian dentist, 'seeing the offender' is hard to reconcile unless the patient had direct repeated exposure to an identified perpetrator; with the rest of the profile focused on generalized danger cues (uniforms, military topics, loud sounds, exits, watching others), this item stands out as clinically implausible for the same trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid evaluation' reflects social/performance-evaluation avoidance, but no threat, trigger, or memory items involve shame, scrutiny, appearance, or performance. It does not fit the otherwise terrorism-focused hypervigilance/trauma-reminder pattern and looks like a strategy for a different symptom cluster.

vignette: Ricardo, a respected dentist of 70, had always found solace in the precise, controlled environment of his practice. That changed two years ago during a visit to his ancestral village in Central America, when a marketplace bombing plunged him into an unimaginable horror. He remembered the deafening blast, the acrid smell of smoke, and the subsequent chaos as local military forces, clad in their distinctive uniforms, rushed into the square. Amidst the screams, he heard a terrifying volley of gunfire, and the sight of his young cousin, a street vendor, falling in the panic became seared into his mind. Pinned down, Ricardo felt an overwhelming surge of helplessness, a profound guilt for not being able to reach or protect his family. After returning to the States, the world Ricardo once knew slowly began to distort. The memory of that day, instead of fading, would return with a terrifying intensity. When the memory came back, it felt completely real across all his senses at once – the smell of dust and cordite, the shouts, the metallic taste of fear – leaving him so overwhelmed by emotion that he would have to stop whatever he was doing, sometimes right in the middle of a dental procedure. He couldn't seem to put the frightening event into words, the visceral experience too raw and fragmented for narrative. This constant, overwhelming reliving of the memory often led him to repeatedly blame himself for what happened, convinced he could have done more, a rumination that only served to keep the memory active and unprocessed. It was precisely this unbidden, sensory-rich return of the past that made him hyper-attuned to any environmental cues that might foreshadow its re-emergence, turning seemingly innocuous details into potent reminders. The world outside his memories also became a minefield. The smallest unexpected or loud sound, like a car backfiring or a dropped tray in his office, now instantly became a gunshot noise in his mind, triggering an immediate and intense rush of fear and putting him on high alert. As a result, he found himself constantly scanning for exits as soon as he entered any room or building, whether it was his own waiting room or a grocery store. He also began watching other people closely, searching for any subtle sign that they might harm him, a pervasive sense of threat that made him interpret innocent actions as potentially hostile. This heightened state of vigilance made him acutely sensitive to any related stimuli, so even the sight of a security guard's uniform or an overheard conversation about military topics could instantly flood his senses with the terror of that day, pulling him back into the full sensory reliving of the bombing. Living in this constant pitch of readiness and pervasive sense of threat meant that almost anything could be perceived as a potential trigger, confirming his inner belief that danger lurked everywhere. Ricardo’s strategies to cope with this constant threat and intrusive memory only seemed to tighten the grip of his fear. Because the memory came back with such vivid, unbidden force, Ricardo found that even the most innocuous sensory inputs—a sudden loud noise, a glimpse of a uniform—could instantly pull him back, making the external world feel dense with reminders of the trauma. Whenever a trigger, like someone mentioning the military, brought back the overwhelming memories, he would retreat further into self-blame, convinced that if he had been stronger or smarter, things would be different. This rumination, a maladaptive strategy he couldn't break free from, paradoxically made the memories even harder to process, keeping them vivid and raw. His pervasive sense of threat, the feeling that danger lurked everywhere, also led him to start carrying a weapon, a small, licensed handgun tucked into his jacket. This act, while intended to make him feel safer, ironically reinforced his belief that the world was a dangerous place and that he needed to be constantly prepared for harm. He also found himself avoiding news reports about events similar to what had happened to him, turning off the television or skipping newspaper sections, which only ensured that any mention of conflict or uniforms caught him off guard, making those triggers even more jarring when they inevitably appeared. The impact on his life was profound. The once bustling dental practice, a source of pride and purpose, now felt like another arena for his hypervigilance. He found it increasingly difficult to focus, often losing his train of thought mid-sentence with a patient, and his once-steady hands would sometimes tremble. His social life, already quiet since his wife’s passing, dwindled further as the exhaustion of constant threat monitoring made him withdraw. He sought help because he could no longer bear the tightening spiral of fear and memory, worried that the man he once was—the calm, capable dentist—was being consumed by the terror of a past he couldn't escape.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not convey that the patient's intrusive memories cause or influence the presence or perception of triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not convey that the patient's sense of threat causes or influences the presence or perception of triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
